variable {α : Sort*} {φ : α → Prop} (h : ∃! x, φ x)
informal_statement: There exists a unique element `h` such that for any `x`, `x` equals `h` if and only if `φ x` holds.
informal_proof:
First, we consider the forward direction of the equivalence: if `x` equals `choose! h`, then `φ x` must hold. By the definition of `choose!`, `choose! h` is the unique element `h` that satisfies `φ x`. Therefore, if `x` equals `choose! h`, it directly follows that `x` satisfies `φ x`.

Next, we consider the reverse direction: if `φ x` holds, then `x` must equal `choose! h`. Given that `choose!` provides a unique element `h` satisfying `φ x`, if `x` also satisfies `φ x`, it follows that `x` must be `h` to maintain uniqueness. Therefore, `x` equals `choose! h`.

This completes the proof of the equivalence.

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
Given that there exists an element satisfying `p`, returns one such element.

This is a straightforward consequence of, and equivalent to, `Classical.choice`.

See also `choose_spec`, which asserts that the returned value has property `p`.
-/
noncomputable def choose {α : Sort u} {p : α → Prop} (h : ∃ x, p x) : α :=
  (indefiniteDescription p h).val
